q: Can a robust, cross-validated genomic-marker panel be built that reliably discriminates A. veronii pathotypes (fish-adapted vs mammalian/human-adapted vs environmental) from draft assemblies alone, and turned into a deployable predictive-virulence-genotype pipeline for aquaculture diagnostic labs?
basis: Tekedar et al. 2019 (PLoS ONE 14(8):e0221018) identify a striking pathotype signature — ML09-123 (US catfish) and TH0426 (China, yellowhead catfish) share ANI > 99.91% and are enriched for T3SS/T6SSi/TssJ (AHA_1837/VasD), while all 7 human isolates in the panel (AVNIH1, AVNIH2, AMC35, AER397, CECT4257, CCM 4359, LMG 13067) lack T3SS and T6SSi. This replication confirmed the pattern for ML09-123, TH0426, and AVNIH1 via BV-BRC Specialty Genes (T3SS hits: 49/68/0; T6SS: 15/15/0), but the classifier itself does not exist in the paper — it is a descriptive comparative-genomics observation on 41 strains, not a validated diagnostic pipeline. BV-BRC now has 726 public A. veronii genomes (2026-07-04), enabling a much larger training/test split than 2019.
next_steps: Pull all 726 A. veronii genomes from BV-BRC + associated metadata (isolation source, host, geography, disease association) and curate labels into fish-clinical / mammalian-clinical / environmental / uncertain classes.
Build a Panaroo or PPanGGOLiN pan-genome on the full 726-genome set and encode gene presence/absence + secretion-system module completeness as features.
Train regularized logistic regression + random forest + gradient boosting classifiers with 5-fold stratified CV blocked by phylogenetic clade (to avoid clade-leakage overestimation).
Externally validate on an independent holdout of any 2025-2026 A. veronii genomes not in the training pool.

Package top-N discriminative markers as a portable, presence/absence PCR/qPCR panel or a MinION-classifier suitable for on-site aquaculture diagnostic labs; benchmark sensitivity/specificity vs whole-genome ground truth.

q: What are the specific genomic determinants that enable A. veronii to jump between fish hosts (catfish, tilapia, carp) and to cause human wound/systemic infections, and what would a one-health surveillance framework need to detect emerging cross-host lineages before outbreaks?
basis: The paper's most provocative single observation, replicated here, is that a US channel-catfish isolate (ML09-123, GCA_002906945.1) and a Chinese yellowhead-catfish isolate (TH0426, GCA_001593245.1) sit at ANI > 99.91% — effectively the same genome on two continents — while the panel's human isolates (AVNIH1 = 654.48 lacks both T3SS and T6SS) sit clearly apart. This raises but does not answer the host-jump question. The paper contains no temporal-phylogenetic signal, no phylogeography, no clinical-vs-fish outbreak-linkage data. Human wound infections with A. veronii are a documented one-health concern, but the paper's 7-human vs 34-non-human split is too small to resolve.
next_steps: Assemble a temporally- and geographically-stratified A. veronii genome set (fish + human + environmental) with sample-collection metadata and reconstruct a dated core-genome phylogeny (BEAST or TreeTime) to test whether cross-continent catfish isolates share a most-recent-common-ancestor within recent aquaculture-trade history.
Perform host-associated GWAS (pyseer or similar) on presence/absence and SNP features vs isolation-host labels to identify variants that recur independently in host-transition events.

Test candidate host-jump genes (adhesins, secretion effectors, iron acquisition, capsule loci) in cross-host virulence assays (catfish → tilapia → murine-wound model) to move from correlation to causation.

Pilot a one-health surveillance framework: quarterly WGS of A. veronii from aquaculture ponds + processing plants + clinical wound-infection isolates in one region (e.g. Mississippi delta or a Chinese carp-farming province), stream to a public dashboard with automated pathotype-classifier + alerting.

q: How much effector-repertoire diversity exists across A. veronii T2SS, T3SS, and T6SS secretion systems at the pan-species level, and which effectors drive pathotype-specific virulence versus environmental fitness (biofilm, competition, iron acquisition)?
basis: Tekedar et al. count 68 secretion-system genes as the dominant virulence category (out of 207 total putative virulence genes across the 41-strain panel) and note that T3SS, T5SS, T6SSi, and TAD are variably present. This replication confirmed the qualitative T3SS/T6SS presence pattern in ML09-123 (49 T3SS-associated products, 15 T6SS) and TH0426 (68/15), and complete absence in AVNIH1 (0/0), plus the marquee shared TssJ/VasD/AHA_1837 lipoprotein in the ML09-123/TH0426 pair. But the paper does not enumerate the effector repertoires beyond a list — the functional split between anti-eukaryotic virulence effectors and inter-bacterial/environmental T6SS effectors is not resolved.
next_steps: Systematically annotate effector repertoires (T3SE, T6SE) across all public A. veronii genomes using dedicated tools (BastionX, T3SE-prediction, SecReT6, Bastion6) with confidence scores.
Cluster effectors into orthologous groups and cross-reference against known anti-eukaryotic vs anti-bacterial effector families in the Aeromonadaceae / Vibrionaceae literature.
Correlate effector presence with pathotype label (fish-clinical, human-clinical, environmental) and biofilm-formation phenotype where isolate collections have matched phenotypic data.

Perform in vitro delivery assays (secretion in T6SS-active conditions) + fish-cell-line cytotoxicity + inter-species competition assays (A. veronii vs Vibrio spp., vs E. coli) for the top-ranked effectors to separate virulence-modulating vs fitness-modulating roles.

q: What is the composition and dynamics of the A. veronii accessory-genome mobilome (plasmids, integrative conjugative elements, prophages, insertion sequences) and how does it drive antimicrobial-resistance-gene horizontal transfer within polymicrobial aquaculture communities (Aeromonas + Vibrio + Enterobacteriaceae)?
basis: The paper explicitly runs ISsaga (insertion sequences), PHASTER (prophages), and CARD (antimicrobial resistance) across the 41-strain panel — this is directly in-scope for the original analysis but the resulting mobilome + AMR-gene numbers were not the paper's headline claims and were not extracted quantitatively in this replication. The paper's open pan-genome (γ = 0.240) and gene-cardinality curves suggest that accessory-genome flux is substantial, but the paper does not characterize the mobilome connectivity to co-resident aquaculture microbiome partners. Aquaculture is a well-documented AMR-selection hotspot (antibiotic prophylaxis, dense stocking) and Aeromonas + Vibrio + Enterobacteriaceae co-inhabit pond sediments and fish gut.
next_steps: Systematically classify each A. veronii accessory contig as plasmid vs ICE vs prophage vs IS-mobilized using MOB-suite, ICEfinder, PHASTER, and ISEScan across the full BV-BRC A. veronii collection.
Build a shared-mobilome network across A. veronii + A. hydrophila + Vibrio anguillarum + Vibrio parahaemolyticus + aquaculture-associated Enterobacteriaceae using k-mer or gene-sharing metrics.
Overlay CARD/ResFinder AMR-gene annotations on the mobilome network to identify AMR genes with active cross-genus movement.

Longitudinally sample one aquaculture site over 12-24 months (pond water + sediment + fish gut + biofilm) with metagenomics + isolate WGS to directly observe HGT events and correlate them with antibiotic-use logs and probiotic co-treatment schedules.

q: How can a genome-based epidemiology surveillance framework for A. veronii be operationalized inside aquaculture health-management programs — integrating antibiotic-stewardship, probiotic co-treatment monitoring, and vaccine-target discovery — to reduce disease burden and AMR emergence at the farm level?
basis: The paper's stated motivation is that A. veronii is a globally important aquaculture pathogen (channel catfish MAS in the SE US, yellowhead catfish outbreaks in China) and the ML09-123/TH0426 pair (ANI > 99.91%, replicated here) is offered as evidence of a globally circulating pathotype. This implicitly argues for surveillance and coordinated intervention, but the paper stops at the descriptive-genomics stage — it does not propose or evaluate a surveillance framework, a vaccine target, or an integration point with existing aquaculture health-management workflows. The pathotype claim is genomic-similarity-only (no cross-host challenge experiments), and the marquee shared TssJ/VasD/AHA_1837 element (verified here in both catfish isolates) is a plausible but untested vaccine-target candidate.
next_steps: Design a pilot farm-level surveillance program at 3-5 catfish/tilapia/carp facilities in the US, Southeast Asia, and Europe: quarterly WGS on A. veronii isolates from routine health checks + mortality events, streamed to a shared dashboard with automated pathotype classification.

Couple isolate WGS with farm-level antibiotic-use logs, probiotic products applied, water-quality/temperature time series, and fish-health-outcome records to build a predictive early-warning model for A. veronii outbreaks.

Prioritize the shared conserved virulence factors (TssJ/VasD/AHA_1837 + adhesins + iron-acquisition surface proteins + conserved T3SS/T6SS structural components) as recombinant subunit vaccine or bacterin-formulation candidates; screen for cross-protective potential using catfish and tilapia challenge models.

Publish a WHO/OIE/FAO-tri-agency-aligned operational playbook that ties the surveillance data feed to antibiotic-stewardship decision rules and vaccination-timing recommendations, with a measurable KPI (reduction in prophylactic antibiotic days per production cycle without loss of survival).
